eventSummary.en: Matthew and Luke place Jesus' birth in Bethlehem, the city of David, before the death of Herod the Great. Luke ties it to a census under Quirinius; Matthew records the magi and the flight to Egypt. The Church of the Nativity (built under Constantine/Justinian over a cave venerated from at least the 2nd c., per Justin Martyr and Origen) marks the traditional grotto. Scholarly birth window is c. 6-4 BC, set by Herod's death (securely c. spring 4 BC via Josephus' lunar-eclipse note of 13 March 4 BC and reign calculations).

title.en: Birth of Jesus in Bethlehem

display.en: boyhood pre-ministry; rejection episode early-mid ministry c. AD 28-30

eventSummary.en: Nazareth was Jesus' hometown (Luke's annunciation; the family's return after Egypt in Matthew). A small agrarian Jewish village (~few hundred people) in the early 1st c., confirmed by IAA excavations (the Nazareth Village Farm, a 1st-c. house near the Church of the Annunciation, wine/olive presses, tombs, and pottery). Jesus taught in its synagogue (Luke 4:16-30) and was rejected ('no prophet is accepted in his hometown'); a cliff is associated with the attempt to throw him down.

title.en: Return to Nazareth

eventSummary.en: Jesus' public ministry opens with his baptism by John in the Jordan and the wilderness temptation. John names the baptism site 'Bethany beyond the Jordan' (John 1:28). Al-Maghtas in Jordan, with Byzantine churches and pilgrimage remains, is the leading candidate and a UNESCO World Heritage Site; Qasr al-Yahud opposite is the western traditional spot.

title.en: Baptism of Jesus at the Jordan

display.en: primary base throughout Galilean ministry c. AD 28-30

eventSummary.en: Capernaum was Jesus' adopted base ('his own city', Matthew 9:1) and home of Peter, Andrew, James and John and Matthew the tax-collector. Many events occur here: healing of Peter's mother-in-law, the paralytic lowered through the roof, the centurion's servant, the synagogue teaching/exorcism, and the Bread of Life discourse (John 6). Archaeology shows a 1st-c. basalt synagogue foundation beneath the later 4th-5th-c. white limestone synagogue, and an octagonal Byzantine church over a 1st-c. house traditionally identified as Peter's. Jesus pronounced woe on it (Matthew 11:23).

title.en: Ministry Headquarters at Capernaum

eventSummary.en: Cana is where John places Jesus' first 'sign', turning water into wine at a wedding (John 2), and the healing of the official's son (John 4:46-54); it is also the home of Nathanael (John 21:2). Site is contested. Khirbet Qana shows continuous Jewish settlement (323 BC-AD 324), a synagogue/study hall, and a pilgrimage veneration cave, making it the strongest archaeological candidate; Kafr Kanna is the medieval-to-modern pilgrim site but lacks demonstrable Roman-era Jewish remains beneath it.

title.en: The Wedding at Cana of Galilee

eventSummary.en: The freshwater lake (~21 km x 13 km, surface ~210 m below sea level) is the geographic heart of the Galilean ministry: calling of fishermen, teaching from boats, stilling of the storm, walking on water, and miraculous catches. A 1st-c. wooden boat ('the Jesus Boat', the Migdal/Ginosar boat) excavated in 1986 is dated c. 100 BC-AD 100 and exemplifies the craft of the period.

title.en: Stilling the Storm on the Sea of Galilee

eventSummary.en: Bethsaida is named as the home of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44) and the setting of the healing of a blind man (Mark 8:22-26) and a feeding-miracle vicinity (Luke 9:10). Jesus cursed it with Chorazin (Matthew 11:21). Two excavated sites contend: et-Tell (large mound, Iron Age and Roman remains, long the favored ID) and el-Araj (on the shore, with 1st-c. Roman material and a Byzantine church, fitting a fishing village better). Excavations at both continue.

title.en: Feeding of the Five Thousand at Bethsaida

eventSummary.en: Chorazin is one of the three towns Jesus condemned for unbelief despite his mighty works (Matthew 11:21; Luke 10:13). The visible basalt town and synagogue (with a carved 'Seat of Moses') are mainly 3rd-4th c., but recent excavation reported 1st-c. pottery and coins beneath the synagogue floor, suggesting an earlier public building of Jesus' era.

title.en: Preaching & Mighty Works at Chorazin

eventSummary.en: On the gentile (eastern/Decapolis) side of the lake, Jesus exorcises 'Legion' into a herd of pigs that rush down a steep bank into the sea (Mark 5). Manuscripts vary between 'Gerasenes', 'Gadarenes', and 'Gergesenes'. Gergesa is traditionally identified with Kursi, where a steep slope meets the shore and a large Byzantine monastery commemorated the miracle. Gadara (Umm Qais) and Gerasa (Jerash) are major Decapolis cities lying farther inland/southeast. Jesus also healed and fed crowds in the Decapolis (Mark 7:31-37; 8:1-10).

title.en: Healing of the Gerasene Demoniac in Decapolis

display.en: mid ministry, northern excursion c. AD 29

eventSummary.en: Jesus withdrew northwest into gentile Phoenician territory ('the region of Tyre and Sidon'), where he healed the daughter of the Syrophoenician/Canaanite woman (Mark 7:24-30; Matthew 15:21-28). Both cities are ancient, securely located Phoenician ports. Tyre lies ~50 km NW of Capernaum; Sidon ~40 km further north.

title.en: Excursion to Tyre and Sidon

display.en: later Galilean ministry, turning point c. AD 29-30

eventSummary.en: At Caesarea Philippi, near the cave-sanctuary of Pan and the springs of the Jordan, Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah and Jesus speaks of building his church and his coming passion (Matthew 16:13-23). The Transfiguration follows about a week later on a 'high mountain' (Matthew 17:1-8), traditionally Mount Tabor but, given proximity, possibly a spur of Mount Hermon. The site preserves the Pan sanctuary niches and Philip's city remains.

title.en: Peter's Confession at Caesarea Philippi

eventSummary.en: Traveling between Judea and Galilee through Samaria, Jesus meets the Samaritan woman at Jacob's Well (John 4), discusses worship 'on this mountain' (Mount Gerizim) versus Jerusalem, and stays two days in Sychar. The deep ancient well (still extant inside the church) and the Samaritan sanctity of Gerizim are well attested.

title.en: The Woman at Jacob's Well (Samaria)

display.en: final journey to Jerusalem, c. days before the last Passover (AD 30 or 33)

eventSummary.en: On the final ascent to Jerusalem for Passover, Jesus passes through Jericho: he heals blind Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46-52) and calls the tax-collector Zacchaeus down from a sycamore-fig (Luke 19:1-10). The NT Roman/Herodian Jericho (Hasmonean-Herodian palace complex at Tulul Abu el-Alayiq) lies near the wadi Qelt, distinct from the prehistoric Tell es-Sultan mound. The road climbs ~1,000 m over ~27 km from Jericho (below sea level) to Jerusalem.

title.en: Encounter with Zacchaeus & Healing at Jericho

display.en: Lazarus shortly before the last Passover; Passion Week c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: Bethany, home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus, is where Jesus raised Lazarus (John 11) and was anointed before the passion (John 12; Mark 14:3-9). It served as his lodging during Passion Week. The Triumphal Entry was staged from neighboring Bethphage. The Tomb of Lazarus has been venerated since at least the 2nd c.; Eusebius notes the village was already called by the Lazarus-name.

title.en: Raising of Lazarus at Bethany

display.en: festival visits across ministry; climactic Passion Week c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: Jerusalem is the destination of Jesus' pilgrim journeys (John records multiple festival visits) and the locus of Passion Week: the cleansing of the Temple, daily teaching in the courts, eschatological discourse, and confrontations with authorities. Herod the Great's vastly expanded Temple platform is archaeologically attested by massive ashlar courses (Western Wall), monumental staircases, and the Trumpeting-Place inscription. The Temple was destroyed by Rome in AD 70.

title.en: Triumphal Entry & Cleansing of the Temple

display.en: Thursday evening before the crucifixion, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: Jesus shares the Last Supper with the Twelve in a furnished upper room (Mark 14; Luke 22), instituting the bread-and-cup remembrance. In the Synoptics this is a Passover meal (Nisan 15); in John the meal precedes Passover (Jesus dies as the lambs are slain on Nisan 14). The traditional Cenacle on Mount Zion is a long-standing but architecturally later commemoration.

title.en: The Last Supper in the Upper Room

display.en: night before the crucifixion, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: After the supper Jesus prays in agony at Gethsemane and is arrested following Judas' betrayal (Mark 14:32-52). The site at the Mount of Olives foot, across the Kidron, fits the Gospel topography; very old olive trees grow there (some radiocarbon/genetic studies date roots to the 12th c., though the locale itself is early-attested by pilgrims).

title.en: Agony in the Garden of Gethsemane

display.en: Friday of the crucifixion, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: Jesus is tried before the Jewish authorities and then Pontius Pilate, who sentences him at a place called Gabbatha/Lithostrotos. Two candidate locations: the older pilgrim tradition (Antonia Fortress, anchoring the Via Dolorosa) and the now widely-favored scholarly view that Pilate, when in Jerusalem, resided and judged at Herod's Palace in the western city. The 'Pilate stone' from Caesarea independently confirms Pontius Pilate as prefect of Judaea.

title.en: The Trial Before Pontius Pilate

display.en: crucifixion Friday 7 April AD 30 or Friday 3 April AD 33 (Nisan 14); resurrection proclaimed the following Sunday

eventSummary.en: Jesus was crucified at Golgotha, died, and was buried in a new rock-cut tomb nearby that belonged to Joseph of Arimathea. On the first day of the week the women found the tomb empty, and the apostles proclaimed that he had risen, “according to the scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). The Church of the Holy Sepulchre is the strongest candidate for both places. Excavations show the area was a disused quarry with first-century rock-cut tombs, outside the city wall in Jesus' day, and Christians remembered it continuously until Constantine built over it in the 4th century. A 2025 report found traces of ancient cultivation beneath the church, which fits John's mention of a garden (John 19:41). The Garden Tomb dates to the Iron Age, centuries earlier, and most archaeologists do not take it as the original tomb.

title.en: Crucifixion, Death & Burial of Jesus

display.en: Journey 1 start c. AD 46-47; Journey 2 start c. AD 49-50

eventSummary.en: Antioch, capital of Roman Syria and one of the largest cities of the empire, was where believers were first called Christians. While its prophets and teachers were fasting and praying, the Holy Spirit said to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work he had called them to. They laid hands on them and sent them off, and the first missionary journey began (Acts 13:1–3).
Paul and Barnabas “went down to Seleucia; and from thence they sailed to Cyprus” (Acts 13:4). Seleucia was Antioch's seaport, about 25 km (16 mi) downriver, founded by Seleucus I around 301 BC.

The first landfall on Cyprus, Barnabas's home island. In Salamis, its chief eastern port, Paul and Barnabas preached the word of God in the Jewish synagogues, with John Mark helping them (Acts 13:5). From here they crossed the whole island to Paphos.

At Paphos, the Roman capital of Cyprus, a sorcerer named Elymas tried to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus away from the faith. Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, declared him blind for a time, and the proconsul believed, “astonished at the teaching of the Lord” (Acts 13:6–12). From here on, Saul is called Paul and leads the mission. Inscriptions from Cyprus name a Paulus as proconsul and confirm that the island was ruled by a proconsul, just as Luke says, though none certainly names this Sergius Paulus.

Sailing from Paphos, the party reached Perga on the coast of Asia Minor, and here John Mark left them and went back to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13). That parting later split Paul and Barnabas. No preaching is recorded on the way in, but on the way home they “preached the word in Perga” (Acts 14:25).

In the synagogue of this Roman colony, Paul preached his first recorded sermon, tracing God's promises from the exodus to David and on to Jesus, raised from the dead (Acts 13:16–41). The next Sabbath almost the whole city came to hear. When opponents drove them out, Paul and Barnabas turned to the Gentiles, and “the word of the Lord was spread abroad throughout all the region” (Acts 13:44–52). They came back later to strengthen the believers and appoint elders (Acts 14:21–23). Excavations since William Ramsay's in 1913–14 have uncovered the city's imperial temple and its gate.

In Iconium Paul and Barnabas spoke so boldly in the synagogue that “a great multitude both of the Jews and also of the Greeks believed” (Acts 14:1). They stayed a long time, and God confirmed the message with signs and wonders. When the divided city plotted to stone them, they fled to Lystra and Derbe (Acts 14:2–6). Iconium is modern Konya, and the living city covers most of the ancient one.

At Lystra Paul healed a man who had never walked, and the crowd shouted in their own language that the gods had come down. They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and the priest of Zeus brought bulls to sacrifice. Paul and Barnabas tore their clothes and pointed them to “the living God, which made heaven, and earth” (Acts 14:8–18). Soon after, opponents from Antioch and Iconium turned the crowd, and Paul was stoned and left for dead. He got up and went back into the city (Acts 14:19–20).

The farthest point of the first journey. Paul and Barnabas “preached the gospel to that city, and had taught many” (Acts 14:21), and no persecution is recorded. Then, instead of going on, they turned back through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch to strengthen the new believers and appoint elders in every church. Gaius, one of Paul's later companions, came from Derbe (Acts 20:4).

After preaching in Perga, they went down to Attalia, the main harbor of Pamphylia, and sailed back to Antioch. There they gathered the church and told how God “had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles” (Acts 14:25–27).

display.en: Journey 1 start c. AD 46-47; Journey 2 start c. AD 49-50

eventSummary.en: The second journey also began at Antioch, after the Jerusalem Council. Paul wanted to revisit the churches, but he and Barnabas disagreed so sharply over taking John Mark that they parted ways. Barnabas took Mark to Cyprus, and Paul chose Silas and set out overland (Acts 15:36–41).

Paul and Silas “went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches” (Acts 15:41). The road likely ran through the mountain pass called the Syrian Gates and past Tarsus, Paul's home city, before it reached Derbe and Lystra.

Back in Lystra, where he had once been stoned, Paul met Timothy, a young believer well spoken of by the brothers there. Paul took him along, and Timothy became one of his closest coworkers (Acts 16:1–3). On this visit the churches were “established in the faith, and increased in number daily” (Acts 16:5).

At Troas, on the Aegean coast, Paul saw a vision in the night: a man of Macedonia pleading, “Come over into Macedonia, and help us” (Acts 16:9). Here the story starts saying “we,” which has long been taken to mean Luke joined the party. From Troas the gospel set sail for Europe.
The ship from Troas stopped overnight at the island of Samothrace and reached Neapolis the next day (Acts 16:11). It was a stop on the voyage, not a place where Paul preached.
Neapolis, the port of Philippi, is where the gospel first came ashore in Europe, as far as Acts records (Acts 16:11). From here the road ran about 16 km inland to Philippi.

In this Roman colony, by a riverside place of prayer, Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, believed and was baptized with her household. Paul and Silas were later beaten and jailed, but at midnight they were praying and singing hymns when an earthquake opened the prison. The jailer asked, “what must I do to be saved?” and his whole household believed (Acts 16:13–34). Paul later wrote this church the letter to the Philippians.

For three Sabbaths Paul reasoned in the synagogue at Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia, showing from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise again. Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and a number of leading women believed. Opponents raised a mob and accused the believers of saying “there is another king, one Jesus” (Acts 17:1–9). Paul later wrote this church 1 and 2 Thessalonians.

Sent away by night, Paul and Silas came to Berea. Its people “received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so,” and many believed (Acts 17:11–12). When agitators followed from Thessalonica, the believers sent Paul on toward Athens while Silas and Timothy stayed.

Paul was stirred to see Athens “wholly given to idolatry.” He reasoned in the synagogue and the marketplace, and the philosophers brought him to the Areopagus. There he told them that the “unknown god” they worshiped is the God who made the world, who has raised Jesus from the dead (Acts 17:16–31). Some mocked, but Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris and others believed (Acts 17:32–34).

Paul stayed a year and a half in Corinth, the capital of Achaia, working as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla. The Lord told him in a vision, “Be not afraid, but speak … for I have much people in this city” (Acts 18:9–10). When opponents brought him before the proconsul Gallio, Gallio threw the case out (Acts 18:12–17). An inscription found at Delphi names this same Gallio and dates to Claudius's reign, about AD 52. It is the firmest anchor for dating Paul's stay in Corinth, though the exact year of Gallio's term is still debated.

At Cenchreae, Corinth's eastern harbor, Paul had his hair cut because of a vow, then sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18:18). Phoebe, whom Paul later commends to the church in Rome, served the church here (Romans 16:1).

On the way home Paul reasoned briefly in the synagogue at Ephesus and left Priscilla and Aquila there. Asked to stay, he promised, “I will return again unto you, if God will” (Acts 18:19–21). He kept that promise on the third journey.
Paul landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the church, most likely in Jerusalem, and then went down to Antioch, ending the second journey (Acts 18:22).
After some time at Antioch, his home church, Paul set out a third time. He went through “all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in order, strengthening all the disciples” (Acts 18:23).

Paul traveled overland through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening the churches he had planted on the first journey and revisited on the second (Acts 18:23). The pin sits at Pisidian Antioch to stand for the whole region.

display.en: AD 52-55 (early chronology) to AD 54-57 (later chronology); roughly 'three years' (Acts 20:31)

eventSummary.en: Paul spent about three years at Ephesus, the heart of the third journey (Acts 20:31). He taught daily in the hall of Tyrannus, so that “all they which dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 19:10). God worked extraordinary miracles through him, and new believers burned their books of magic in public (Acts 19:11–19). His stay ended in a riot led by the silversmith Demetrius, who feared for the trade around the goddess Artemis (Acts 19:23–41). Paul probably wrote 1 Corinthians here (1 Corinthians 16:8).

display.en: AD 55-57 (late autumn through following spring; varies by chronology)

eventSummary.en: After the riot, Paul left for Macedonia, encouraging the churches there, and then spent three months in Greece (Acts 20:1–3). He probably wrote 2 Corinthians from Macedonia and Romans from Corinth during this time, while gathering a gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem. The pin sits at Philippi to stand for the region.

display.en: Spring AD 57 (late chronology) / 56 (early chronology), around Passover/Unleavened Bread

eventSummary.en: At Troas the believers gathered on the first day of the week to break bread, and Paul talked until midnight. A young man named Eutychus fell asleep in a third-story window and fell to his death. Paul went down, embraced him and said, “Trouble not yourselves; for his life is in him,” and they took the young man home alive (Acts 20:7–12).

Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul sent for the elders of Ephesus to meet him at Miletus. In his farewell he told them to shepherd the church of God, “which he hath purchased with his own blood,” and reminded them of Jesus' words, “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts 20:17–35). They knelt, prayed and wept, knowing they would not see him again (Acts 20:36–38).

At Caesarea the party stayed with Philip the evangelist. The prophet Agabus bound his own hands and feet with Paul's belt and warned that Paul would be bound in Jerusalem. Paul answered, “I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 21:8–14).

In Jerusalem Paul reported to James and the elders what God had done among the Gentiles (Acts 21:17–26). Days later a crowd in the temple accused him of bringing Greeks inside, and the Roman tribune arrested him to stop the riot (Acts 21:27–36). Paul told the crowd his own story of meeting Jesus (Acts 22), stood before the Sanhedrin (Acts 23:1–10), and escaped a plot by more than forty men when his nephew warned the tribune. He was then sent under heavy guard by night to Caesarea (Acts 23:12–33).

display.en: c. AD 57-59 (early chronology) or AD 58-60 (later chronology); 'two years' (Acts 24:27)

eventSummary.en: Paul was held about two years in Herod's palace at Caesarea. The governor Felix heard his case, hoped for a bribe, and left him in chains (Acts 24). When Festus took over, Paul refused to be sent back to Jerusalem and used his right as a Roman citizen: “I appeal unto Caesar” (Acts 25:11). He then told his story before King Agrippa II and Bernice, who agreed he had done nothing to deserve death. Agrippa said he could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:13–26:32).

Paul, with other prisoners, was handed to a centurion named Julius of the Augustan Cohort and embarked on a ship of Adramyttium (Acts 27:1-2). Luke and Aristarchus accompanied him (a 'we'-passage). The next day they put in at Sidon, where Julius kindly allowed Paul to visit friends and be cared for (27:3).

Because of contrary winds they sailed under the lee (sheltered side) of Cyprus, then across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, landing at Myra in Lycia (Acts 27:4-5). There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship (a grain freighter) bound for Italy and transferred the prisoners onto it (27:6). Myra was a known port on the Alexandria-to-Rome grain route.

display.en: Autumn AD 59 / 57 (after the Day of Atonement 'fast', Acts 27:9)

eventSummary.en: Sailing slowly against the wind, the ship reached Cnidus with difficulty, then ran under the lee of Crete off Cape Salmone, and arrived at Fair Havens near the city of Lasea (Acts 27:7-8). The coordinates given are for Fair Havens (Kaloi Limenes). 'Much time had been lost and the voyage was now dangerous because the Fast (Yom Kippur, ~late September/October) had already gone by' (27:9). Paul warned against sailing on, but the centurion followed the pilot and owner; since the harbor was unsuitable to winter in, the majority decided to try to reach Phoenix, a better Cretan harbor (27:10-12).

Attempting to reach Phoenix, a Cretan harbor 'facing southwest and northwest' (Acts 27:12), the ship was caught by a violent northeasterly wind called Euraquilo (Euroclydon; a Greek-Latin compound for the ENE wind, attested on a Roman wind-rose in Tunisia). Driven past the small island of Cauda (Clauda/Gavdos), the crew undergirded the hull with cables, lowered gear, jettisoned cargo and tackle, and lost sight of sun and stars for many days (27:13-20). Paul, after an angelic vision, assured all 276 aboard that no life would be lost, only the ship (27:21-26).

On the fourteenth night of the storm, the sailors sensed land and ran the ship aground at dawn. The stern broke apart, but all 276 people on board reached shore safely, just as God had promised Paul (Acts 27:27–44). The island was Malta. Its people built a fire and welcomed them. A viper fastened on Paul's hand and did him no harm. Paul healed the father of Publius, the island's chief man, and then the rest of the sick who came to him (Acts 28:1–9).

After three months they sailed on another Alexandrian grain ship with the figurehead of the Twin Brothers (Castor and Pollux, the Dioscuri). They put in at Syracuse (3 days), then Rhegium, and with a favorable south wind reached Puteoli in one more day (Acts 28:11-13). At Puteoli they found believers and stayed seven days, then headed toward Rome. Coordinates given are for Puteoli (Pozzuoli).

Roman believers came out to meet Paul at the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns on the Via Appia (Acts 28:15). In Rome Paul was allowed to live by himself under guard (light custody/house arrest). He met the local Jewish leaders, expounded the kingdom of God and Jesus from the Law and Prophets (28:17-28), and 'lived there two whole years at his own expense, welcoming all who came, preaching the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance' (28:30-31). Acts ends here, abruptly, without recording the trial's outcome.

Early Sunday morning, Mary Magdalene and other women came to anoint the body and found the stone rolled away, the tomb empty, and angels announcing the resurrection. Mary Magdalene, remaining at the tomb weeping, encountered the risen Jesus — mistaking him for the gardener until he said her name, 'Mary!' (John 20:11-18). He told her, 'Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father.' As the women hurried to tell the disciples, Jesus met them; they clasped his feet and worshiped (Matthew 28:9-10). The same day, the Lord also appeared to Peter alone (Luke 24:34; 1 Corinthians 15:5), though no narrative details are given. The 2016-2017 restoration of the Edicule by the National Technical University of Athens confirmed the original 1st-c. limestone burial bench is intact. Sapienza University excavations found ancient olive-tree and grapevine traces beneath the floor, consistent with John 19:41 ('in the place where he was crucified there was a garden, and in the garden a new tomb').

title.en: Resurrection & Empty Tomb Appearances

display.en: Easter Sunday afternoon, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: Two disciples — one named Cleopas, the other unnamed — walked from Jerusalem to Emmaus (~60 stadia / ~11 km in most manuscripts; ~160 stadia / ~30 km in Codex Sinaiticus). A stranger joined them and, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, explained 'the things concerning himself' in all the Scriptures. At supper in Emmaus, 'he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight' (Luke 24:30-31). They exclaimed, 'Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the Scriptures?' and returned immediately to Jerusalem to tell the Eleven. The Emmaus-Nicopolis identification (Amwas/Latrun) has Byzantine basilica ruins and attestation by Eusebius (c. AD 330); el-Qubeibeh is the Franciscan traditional site since the 15th century.

title.en: Appearance on the Road to Emmaus

display.en: Easter Sunday evening, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: That evening the disciples gathered behind locked doors 'for fear of the Jews.' Jesus appeared in their midst and said, 'Peace be with you.' He showed them his hands and side, breathed on them and said, 'Receive the Holy Spirit' (John 20:19-23). He ate a piece of broiled fish to demonstrate his physical, bodily reality (Luke 24:36-43). Thomas was absent and later refused to believe: 'Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and place my finger into the mark of the nails, and place my hand into his side, I will never believe' (John 20:25). Epiphanius (4th c.) mentions a 'Church of the Apostles' on Mount Zion that survived the AD 70 destruction; archaeologist Bargil Pixner argued for a Judeo-Christian synagogue or house church predating the current medieval Cenacle structure.

title.en: Easter Evening Appearance in the Upper Room

display.en: one week after Easter, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: Eight days later (the following Sunday), the disciples were again in the locked room, this time with Thomas present. Jesus appeared, stood among them, and said to Thomas, 'Put your finger here, and see my hands; and put out your hand, and place it in my side. Do not disbelieve, but believe.' Thomas exclaimed, 'My Lord and my God!' (Greek: ho kyrios mou kai ho theos mou) — the highest christological declaration in the Gospels. Jesus replied, 'Have you believed because you have seen me? Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed' (John 20:26-29). This bridges to all subsequent faith beyond the eyewitness generation.

title.en: Appearance to Thomas Eight Days Later

display.en: during the 40 days before Ascension, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: John 21 records Jesus' third appearance to the disciples as a group, at the Sea of Tiberias (Galilee). Seven disciples — Peter, Thomas, Nathanael of Cana, James and John (sons of Zebedee), and two unnamed — fished all night and caught nothing. At dawn, Jesus stood on the shore (unrecognized) and told them to cast on the right side; they caught 153 large fish and could not haul the net in. The 'disciple whom Jesus loved' recognized Jesus; Peter jumped into the water and swam to shore. Jesus had a charcoal fire (Greek: anthrakia — the same word as at Peter's denial, John 18:18) with fish and bread ready. After breakfast, Jesus three times asked Peter, 'Do you love me?' — one restoration for each denial — and commissioned him: 'Feed my sheep.' He also prophesied Peter's martyrdom (John 21:18-19). The Church of the Primacy of St. Peter at Tabgha preserves the Mensa Christi (flat rock) over 4th-c. Byzantine foundations. The 1st-c. 'Jesus Boat' from nearby Ginosar exemplifies the fishing craft of the period.

title.en: Miraculous Catch of 153 Fish at Galilee

display.en: during the 40 days before Ascension, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: The Eleven went to the mountain in Galilee 'to which Jesus had directed them' (Matthew 28:16). When they saw him, they worshiped, though 'some doubted.' Jesus declared: 'All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age' (Matthew 28:18-20). Many scholars associate the appearance to 'more than 500 brothers at one time, most of whom are still alive' (1 Corinthians 15:6) with this Galilean mountain gathering, as it is the only large-scale outdoor post-resurrection event. Paul wrote c. AD 53-55; his note about surviving witnesses is an implicit invitation to verify. The 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 creed is dated by virtually all critical scholars — including skeptics Gerd Lüdemann and Bart Ehrman — to within 3-6 years of the crucifixion, making it the earliest datable testimony to the resurrection appearances.

disputes.en: The mountain in Galilee is not named in the Gospel accounts. Mount Tabor is the traditional site, while Mount Arbel is a popular alternative overlooking the Sea of Galilee.

title.en: The Great Commission on the Mountain

display.en: during the 40 days before Ascension, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: Paul's creedal summary records that Jesus 'appeared to James, then to all the apostles' (1 Corinthians 15:7). No narrative details are given in the New Testament. James — the brother of Jesus, not James son of Zebedee — was skeptical during the ministry ('not even his brothers believed in him', John 7:5) but became the leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). This transformation from skeptic to martyr-leader is most naturally explained by a post-resurrection appearance. The lost Gospel of the Hebrews (quoted by Jerome) preserves a tradition that James had vowed not to eat until he saw the risen Lord. Josephus independently records the execution of 'James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ' in AD 62 (Antiquities 20.9.1), confirming both James's existence and his identification as Jesus's brother. The location of this appearance is not specified; Jerusalem is assumed as the base of James's subsequent ministry.

title.en: Appearance to James in Jerusalem

display.en: 40 days after the resurrection, c. AD 30 or 33

eventSummary.en: Forty days after the resurrection (Acts 1:3), Jesus led the apostles out to the Mount of Olives, near Bethany. Over those 40 days he had appeared to them repeatedly, 'speaking about the kingdom of God' and 'presenting himself alive after his suffering by many proofs' (Acts 1:3). He gave final instructions: 'You will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth' (Acts 1:8). 'And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight' (Acts 1:9). Two men in white appeared and said, 'This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven' (Acts 1:11). The disciples returned to Jerusalem from Olivet, 'a Sabbath day's journey away' (~2,000 cubits, ~1 km). The Chapel of the Ascension has been venerated since the Bordeaux Pilgrim (AD 333); the original Imbomon rotunda was built c. AD 378-384 by Poimenia, destroyed in AD 614, rebuilt by Crusaders, and converted to a mosque by Saladin (1187).

title.en: The Ascension from Mount Olivet

eventSummary.en: During his trial before the Sanhedrin, Stephen — the first Christian martyr — 'full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God' (Acts 7:55). Notably, Jesus is described as standing (not seated, as in other passages), possibly signifying welcome or advocacy. Stephen reported the vision aloud; the council rushed him, dragged him outside the city, and stoned him. As he died, he prayed, 'Lord Jesus, receive my spirit' and 'Lord, do not hold this sin against them.' Saul of Tarsus (later Paul) watched, approving the execution (Acts 7:58; 8:1). This is a vision rather than a bodily appearance. The traditional stoning site is near St. Stephen's Gate (Lions' Gate) on Jerusalem's eastern wall; the 5th-c. Basilica of St. Stephen (now Saint-Étienne, within the École Biblique grounds) commemorates the northern tradition.

title.en: Stephen's Vision & Martyrdom in Jerusalem

eventSummary.en: Saul of Tarsus, carrying letters from the high priest to arrest Christians in Damascus, encountered the risen Jesus near the city. 'Suddenly a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?' (Acts 26:13-14). Blinded for three days, he was led to 'the house of Judas on the street called Straight' (Acts 9:11), where Ananias healed and baptized him. Three separate accounts in Acts (chs. 9, 22, 26) plus Paul's own first-person testimony in 1 Corinthians 9:1 ('Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?'), 1 Corinthians 15:8 ('Last of all, as to one untimely born, he appeared also to me'), and Galatians 1:15-16 attest this encounter. Paul's testimony, written c. AD 53-55, is ~20-25 years after the event. The Via Recta ('Straight Street') still follows the exact route of the 1st-c. Roman decumanus maximus. The underground Chapel of Ananias near Bab Sharqi preserves 5th/6th-c. Byzantine church remains (excavated 1921). Paul's basket escape through the wall (Acts 9:25; 2 Corinthians 11:33) is commemorated at the Chapel of St. Paul at Bab Kisan. Even non-Christian scholars treat Paul's radical transformation from persecutor to apostle as historically certain.

title.en: Paul's Vision on the Damascus Road

eventSummary.en: John, exiled to Patmos 'because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus' (Revelation 1:9), was 'in the Spirit on the Lord's day' when he heard a loud voice and, turning, saw the risen Christ glorified among seven golden lampstands: 'one like a son of man, clothed with a long robe... his eyes were like a flame of fire, his feet were like burnished bronze... and his voice was like the roar of many waters' (Revelation 1:12-16). John fell at his feet 'as though dead,' but Jesus laid his right hand on him and said, 'Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades' (Revelation 1:17-18). He commanded John to write the visions and dictated seven letters to the churches of Asia (Revelation 2-3). The Domitianic dating rests on Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3, c. AD 180). The Cave of the Apocalypse and the Monastery of St. John the Theologian (founded AD 1088) are UNESCO World Heritage Sites (inscribed 1999). The identity of 'John' — apostle, elder, or another figure — is itself debated.

title.en: John's Vision of Christ on Patmos
